name: John Snow
title: Trace an outbreak
classification: Reconstructed educational map · synthetic counts · approximate street schematic
problem: Which water source is most strongly implicated by the available evidence?
context: In 1854 Soho, Snow investigated water exposure while many attributed cholera to bad air. His reasoning combined records, interviews, and comparisons.
evidence: Thirty synthetic household locations and three pumps. Coordinates are arbitrary drawing units, not original addresses or a georeferenced historical map.
application: Plan an exposure investigation with public-health teams, considering alternative explanations and population denominators.
reflection: What additional exposure evidence would strengthen or weaken your hypothesis?
assessment: Record a hypothesis, inspect at least two pumps, and discuss exposure and confounding.

name: Florence Nightingale
title: Make mortality patterns visible
classification: Synthetic educational mortality counts · not Crimean War records
problem: Which cause dominates, and does the visual encoding communicate it accurately?
context: Nightingale used mortality records and statistical graphics in her campaign for sanitary reform. Many people and institutional changes contributed to reform.
evidence: Six invented monthly counts for disease, wounds, and other causes, with exact values in the table.
application: Compare categories and communicate priorities without confusing counts with rates or overstating a chart’s policy effect.
reflection: What population or exposure data would you need to compare mortality risks?
assessment: Explain the main pattern and why polar radii use square roots.

name: Thomas Bayes
title: Update a belief
problem: Estimate P(condition | positive) before calculating it.
context: Bayes’s work, published posthumously with Richard Price’s contribution, became part of the foundations of Bayesian inference.
evidence: Adjustable prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, and expected population counts. This is a probability exercise.
application: Reason about evidence and base rates in quality checks, research, and screening models.
reflection: Why can a highly sensitive test still have a low positive predictive value?
assessment: Compare an initial estimate with the calculated posterior and explain assumptions.

name: Alan Turing
title: Follow an algorithm
classification: Mathematical teaching model · not a historical machine reconstruction
problem: Predict how a tape changes under a transition table.
context: Turing’s 1936 paper formalized an abstract model of computation and investigated the limits of algorithmic procedures.
evidence: Binary increment, unary append, and symbol replacement programs with explicit states and transitions.
application: Debug programs by tracing instructions, state, and edge cases.
reflection: How does a transition table differ from a claim that every problem is computable?
assessment: Predict an output and inspect the transition that leads to halting.

name: Claude Shannon
title: Measure uncertainty
problem: Which distribution is more uncertain, and what happens when the channel is noisy?
context: Shannon’s 1948 theory quantified information and reliable communication in the presence of noise.
evidence: A binary symbol distribution, its entropy, fixed binary symbols, and a reproducible noisy channel.
application: Think about coding, compression, and communication capacity. Entropy measures uncertainty under a model, not truth or meaning.
reflection: Why does a balanced binary source have more entropy than a predictable source?
assessment: Compare two distributions and explain the zero-probability convention.

name: John Tukey
title: Explore before modelling
problem: Does the mean describe a dataset containing an extreme value?
context: Tukey emphasized exploratory examination of data and graphical tools that reveal patterns deserving further inquiry.
evidence: Small editable datasets displayed as a histogram, box plot, and index-value scatter plot.
application: Inspect distributions, errors, missingness, and outliers before fitting a model.
reflection: Is an IQR-flagged value necessarily an error? What would you investigate?
assessment: Compare the mean and median and explain whether flagged observations should be removed.

name: W. Edwards Deming
title: Study process variation
problem: Does the monitoring sequence suggest a change relative to a fixed baseline?
context: Deming helped popularize statistical quality thinking, drawing on a tradition that includes Walter Shewhart’s control charts.
evidence: Twenty baseline observations followed by generated monitoring observations. Limits remain fixed from the baseline.
application: Investigate signals in a process without changing settings in response to every random fluctuation.
reflection: Why is a point outside a control limit a signal for investigation rather than proof of a cause?
assessment: Compare stable and shifted sequences against the baseline and describe uncertainty.

name: Judea Pearl
title: Question a correlation
classification: Mathematical structural causal model · synthetic probabilities
problem: How can observational association differ from an intervention?
context: Pearl developed graphical frameworks for causal reasoning in which conclusions depend on explicitly stated structural assumptions.
evidence: Predefined confounder, mediator, and collider diagrams with toy structural equations.
application: Design studies and state causal assumptions before interpreting associations.
reflection: When could controlling for a variable introduce rather than remove bias?
assessment: Identify a variable’s role and compare observation with intervention under the specified model.
